newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's electric firms boosted by owner changes.
newsitem.headline: Spain's electric firms boosted by owner changes.

text.p: Shares in Spanish electricity firms should continue to surge as a rash of purchases levels out differences between the companies and prepares them for new regulation, analysts said on Monday.

"The (new) groups will be levelled out in terms of their distribution and generating set-up and mix and the changes should be beneficial to the sector," said a utilities analyst at a Spanish brokerage, who asked not to be named.

However, analysts were reluctant to estimate the upside potential for the share prices of the companies concerned. They predicted volatility until details of stake sales are clarified and new legislation governing the sector is confirmed.
Unconfirmed press reports on Monday said Hidrocantabrico was mulling the purchase of a stake in Electra de Viesgo and Saltos del Nansa from Endesa.
As a precautionary measure, the stock exchange commission CNMV suspended shares in Cantabrico, Viesgo and Nansa pending more information.
Analysts said it seemed likely that the sale would go through, although Endesa later denied it intended to sell its stake in the two firms.
If it does go ahead, the purchase would convert Cantabrico into the fourth largest electricity group under the new set-up.

"Previously Cantabrico was primarily a generator, and highly dependent on coal. If it is confirmed (that it is to buy Viesgo and Nansa) it will benefit because not only will it gain distribution quota but also it will have hydro potential. Its generating mix will improve," the analyst said.
On Friday Endesa, which is 66 percent state-owned, launched a friendly bid for up to 75 percent of regional electric utilities Fuerzas Electricas de Catalunya (Fecsa) and Sevillana de Electricidad.
Sevillana and Fecsa remained suspended from trading on the stock exchange on Monday.
Endesa was up 20 pesetas at 8,230 at 1240 GMT and was seen gaining further ground, despite market doubts on how much debt it would need to take on in order to pay for the purchases.

"I think the (sector) operation is positive, particularly for Endesa. I'm not worried (about its debt position) as it generates sufficient resources to cover its needs, and the sale of its stake in Fenosa, Viesgo and Nansa would reduce its debt," said Patricia Fernandez, analyst at Benito y Monjardin.
Speculation on how Endesa's near-eight percent stake in Union Fenosa might be sold and to whom pushed its share price up 18 pesetas to 882 at 1240 GMT.
"There's talk about selling the stake in Fenosa to (savings banks) Cajamadrid and Caixa Galicia, which should be positive for the share price," said one analyst.

The new structure of the sector would thus be made up of four groups. Giants Endesa and Iberdrola would take up 80 percent of the market, the new Fenosa group would account for around 15 percent and the Cantabrico group would take up the rest, analysts said.
